Bechorot 1:1: It is a positive commandment to set apart every male firstborn, the first issue of the womb, whether among humans, among clean animals, or among the species of donkey, whether they are whole or are terefot (afflicted with a condition that would cause them to die within twelve months). As it is stated (Exodus 13:2): "Sanctify to Me every firstborn, the first issue of every womb among the children of Israel, among man and among beast." And all of them belong to the kohanim.
Bechorot 6:1: It is a positive commandment to set apart one out of every ten of all the pure (tahor) animals born to a person each year. This commandment applies only to cattle and sheep or goats, as it is stated (Vayikra 27:32): "And every tithe of the herd or the flock," etc.
Chagigah 1:1:
Three positive commandments were commanded to Israel on each of the three pilgrimage festivals, and they are these: appearing (re'iyah), as it is said, "All your males shall appear"; the festival offering (chagigah), as it is said, "You shall celebrate a festival to Hashem your God"; and rejoicing (simchah), as it is said, "And you shall rejoice in your festival."

The appearing stated in the Torah is that one appears in the Azarah (the Temple courtyard) on the first day of the festival and brings with him an olah offering, whether from fowl or from livestock. One who came to the Azarah on the first day and did not bring an olah has not only failed to fulfill a positive commandment, but also transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said, "My face shall not be seen empty-handed." He does not receive lashes for this prohibition, since he performed no action.

The chagigah stated in the Torah is that one brings shelamim on the first day of the festival when he comes to appear. It is well known that shelamim come only from livestock. Women are not obligated in these two commandments, appearing and the chagigah.

The rejoicing stated regarding the festivals is that one brings shelamim in addition to the shelamim of the chagigah. These are called shalmei simchat chagigah (shelamim of festival rejoicing), as it is said, "And you shall slaughter shelamim, and you shall eat there, and you shall rejoice before Hashem your God." Women are obligated in this commandment.
Korban Pesach 10:12:
When the Pesach offering is brought in the first month (Nisan), a shelamim offering is brought with it on the fourteenth day, from the cattle or from the flock, adult or young, male or female, like all shelamim offerings. This is called the chagigah of the fourteenth, and concerning it the Torah says (Deuteronomy 16:2): "And you shall sacrifice the Pesach offering to Hashem your God, from the flock and the herd."

When is this chagigah brought with it? When the Pesach offering is brought on a weekday (chol), in a state of purity, and when the group is small in number. But if the fourteenth falls on Shabbat, or the Pesach offering is brought in a state of tumah (impurity), or the Pesach offerings are numerous, no chagigah is brought with it, and only the Pesach offerings alone are sacrificed.
Korban Pesach 1:1: It is a positive commandment to slaughter the Pesach offering on the fourteenth of the month of Nisan, after midday. One may slaughter only from the sheep or from the goats, and only a male in its first year. Both men and women are obligated in this commandment.
Korban Pesach 5:1:
One who was tamei (ritually impure) at the time of the slaughter of the Pesach offering, so that it is not slaughtered on his behalf, or who was on a distant journey, or who was prevented by some other circumstance beyond his control, or who erred and did not offer it at the first time, brings a Pesach offering on the fourteenth of the second month, in the afternoon (bein ha'arbayim).

The slaughter of this Pesach offering is a separate positive commandment in its own right, and it overrides Shabbat. For the second Pesach is not a make-up for the first, but a festival in its own right. Therefore, one is liable to karet (excision) for [neglecting] it.
Korban Pesach 8:1: Eating the flesh of the Pesach offering on the night of the fifteenth [of Nisan] is a positive commandment, as it is stated (Exodus 12:8): "They shall eat the flesh on that night, roasted over fire; with matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it."
Korban Pesach 8:15: We have already explained in several places that the Pesach offering is eaten only until midnight, in order to keep a person far from transgression, although the strict law of the Torah is that it may be eaten the entire night, until the dawn rises. We have also already explained in the laws of chametz and matzah that it requires the recitation of Hallel at the time of its eating, and that the members of the group may not resume eating after they have fallen asleep, even at the beginning of the night.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:1: Eating the chatat and the asham is a positive commandment, as it is stated (Shemot 29:33): "And they shall eat those things with which atonement was made." The kohanim eat, and the owners receive atonement. The same applies to the other sacrificial offerings that the kohanim eat: eating them is a mitzvah.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:5: Likewise, the bechor (firstborn animal): concerning it Scripture says (Bamidbar 18:18), "And their flesh shall be yours, like the breast of the wave-offering and like the right thigh." All of these that are eaten by the kohanim are eaten also by the kohanim's slaves and their wives, as with terumah. All of them are eaten anywhere in the city, as it is stated (Vayikra 10:14), "The breast of the wave-offering and the thigh of the raised-offering you shall eat in a tahor place." Scripture did not say of them "in a holy place," meaning the Azarah, but rather "tahor," meaning the entire camp of Israel, which corresponds, for later generations, to Yerushalayim. The same law applies to maaser (the animal tithe) and to the Pesach offering, for they are kodashim kalim like shelamim. The windows and the thickness of the wall are treated as the inside.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:6: Shelamim (peace offerings) may be eaten on the day of the slaughtering, throughout the entire night, and throughout the following day until sunset, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:16): "On the day he offers his sacrifice it shall be eaten, and on the next day," and (Vayikra 7:18): "If any of the flesh of his shelamim sacrifice is eaten on the third day," etc. You therefore learn that they may be eaten for two days and one night, whether it is the portion of the kohanim or the portion of the owners. The same applies to the bechor (firstborn animal) and the maaser (animal tithe), since they are kodashim kalim (offerings of lesser sanctity), like shelamim.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:6-7:
The shelamim (peace offerings) are eaten on the day of the slaughter, throughout the entire night, and throughout the following day until sunset, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:16): "On the day he brings near his sacrifice it shall be eaten, and on the next day"; and (Vayikra 7:18): "And if any of the flesh of his shelamim sacrifice is eaten on the third day," etc. You thus learn that they are eaten for two days and one night, both the portion of the kohanim and the portion of the owners. The same applies to the bechor (firstborn animal) and the maaser (animal tithe), for they are kodashim kalim (offerings of lesser sanctity) like the shelamim.

But the todah (thanksgiving offering), even though it is among the kodashim kalim, is eaten only on the day of the slaughter together with the night, as it is stated regarding it (Vayikra 7:15): "On the day of his offering it shall be eaten; he shall not leave any of it until morning." Similarly, the ram of the nazir and the bread that comes with them, and the like, whether the portion of the kohanim or the portion of the owners, are eaten only for a day and a night. The same applies to the chatat (sin offering), the asham (guilt offering), the shelamim of the tzibur (community), and the remainder of the menachot (meal offerings): all of them are eaten for a day and a night, for it is stated, "On the day of his offering it shall be eaten," which by its implication includes all offerings, except for the shelamim, regarding which the verse specified otherwise, and the bechor and maaser, which are similar to them.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:7:
But the todah (thanksgiving offering), even though it is kodashim kalim (offerings of lesser sanctity), may be eaten only on the day of the slaughtering together with the night [that follows], as it is stated regarding it (Vayikra 7:15): "On the day of its offering it shall be eaten; he shall not leave any of it until morning." Similarly, the ram of the nazir and the bread that accompanies them, and the like, whether the portion of the kohanim or the portion of the owners [is concerned], [may be eaten only for a day and a night].

The same applies to the chatat, the asham, the shelamim of the tzibur (community), and the remainders of the menachot (meal offerings): all of them are eaten for a day and a night, as it is stated, "On the day of its offering it shall be eaten," which by implication includes all offerings, except for the shelamim of the yachid (individual), regarding which the verse specified [otherwise], and the bechor (firstborn animal) and the maaser (animal tithe), which are similar to them.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 12:12: For all women married to kohanim, whether a kohenet (a daughter of a kohen) or a Yisraelit, the remainders of their menachot are not eaten, because of the husband's share, since he may not eat it. Nor is the entire mincha burned on the fires of the Altar, because of the woman's share. Rather, the kometz (the handful) is offered by itself, and the remainders are scattered on the beit hadeshen (the place of the ashes). The kemitzah (taking of the handful) may be done anywhere in the Azarah (Temple courtyard); and if he took the handful in the Heichal (the Sanctuary building), it is valid.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 12:6: All the mincha offerings that are offered upon the Altar require presentation (hagashah) at the west side, opposite the tip of the southwestern corner, and they do not require waving (tenufah). The exceptions are the mincha of a sotah (a woman suspected of infidelity) and the Omer of waving, both of which require waving and presentation.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 12:7: All the menachot (meal offerings) that are offered on the Altar require oil and frankincense: a log of oil for each issaron, and a kometz (handful) of frankincense for each mincha, whether it was a single issaron or sixty issarons, for one does not bring more than sixty issarons in a single vessel, as will be explained. The exceptions are the mincha of jealousy (of a sotah) and the mincha of a sinner, as it is stated (Vayikra 5:11), "He shall not put oil upon it, nor place frankincense upon it."
Maaseh HaKorbanot 12:8: If he put [oil or frankincense on it] and offered it, he receives lashes for the oil by itself and for the frankincense by itself. If he placed a vessel contain
Maaseh HaKorbanot 13:13: How does one scoop (the kometz) of the minchot that are scooped? As any person ordinarily scoops: he spreads his fingers over the palm of his hand and scoops. If he scooped with the tips of his fingers or from the sides, he should not burn it on the altar; but if he burned it, it is accepted. If he added to the scoop, for example, if he spread his fingers apart and scooped, it is invalid.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 14:1:
A person may donate (as a nedavah) or vow an olah, shelamim, and any of the five types of mincha offerings that come as a vow or a freewill offering, whichever type he wishes. He may also donate or vow a mincha consisting only of the mincha of libations (minchat nesachim), of whichever of the three types of libation mincha he chooses, as we have explained. He may also donate or vow wine by itself, or frankincense by itself, or oil by itself, or wood for the arrangement of the altar fire (ma'arachah), because these are like a korban, as it is stated (Nechemiah 10:35): "and for the wood offering (korban ha'etzim)."

Note on the verse citation: the Hebrew text as given cites Nechemiah 13:31; the quoted phrase "u'lekurban ha'etzim" appears there.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:1: All the korbanot of living creatures come from only five species: from cattle, from sheep, from goats, from turtledoves, and from young doves.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:11:
Shelamim offerings come from sheep, from goats, and from cattle; from males and from females; from adult animals and from young ones. Birds, however, are not brought as shelamim.

"Young" animals are those from eight days old until a full year, from day to day. If the year was intercalated, it is intercalated for the animal as well. "Adult" cattle are those up to three full years, from day to day; and among the flock, up to two full years, from day to day. Beyond this, the animal is considered old, and it may not be offered.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:12: Although all korbanot are valid from the eighth day onward, one may not bring them l'chatchilah (initially, ab initio) until the thirtieth day onward. The exceptions are the bechor (firstborn animal), the Pesach offering, and the ma'aser (animal tithe): if one wishes to offer them on the eighth day, he may offer them l'chatchilah.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:14: Anywhere the Torah says *keves* (male lamb), *kisvah* (female lamb), or *kevasim* (lambs), it means animals one year old. Anywhere it says *ayil* or *eilim* (ram or rams), it
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:15:
All communal korbanot are male. Likewise, the chatat offerings of the tzibur (community) come from goats or from cattle; none of them come from sheep. All communal olot come from sheep and from cattle; there is no communal olah from goats.

Every individual's chatat is female and is eaten by the kohanim, and it does not come from cattle, except for three chatat offerings: the chatat of a nasi (leader), which is a goat and is eaten; the chatat of the kohen mashiach (anointed kohen), which is a bull and is burned, and this is the bull that comes for [a transgression of] any of the mitzvot; and the third is the bull that the kohen gadol brings on Yom Kippur, which is a chatat and is burned.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:16: All chatat offerings of the tzibur (community) are eaten, except for the goat of Yom Kippur, whose counterpart is sent away. Likewise, the goats of idolatry and the bull of he'elem (a ruling overlooked by the court) are burned. The bull that comes for any of the mitzvot and the bull of he'elem are called "the bulls that are burned," and the goats of idolatry are called "the goats that are burned." From this you learn that there are five chatat off
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:17: All of these korbanot are called zevachim (sacrifices). All the olot, chatatot, and ashamot, as well as the two lambs of the shelamim of Atzeret (Shavuot), are called kodshei kodashim (offerings of the highest sanctity). But the shelamim of an individual, the bechor (firstborn animal), the maaser (animal tithe), and the Pesach offering are called kodashim kalim (offerings of lesser sanctity).
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:2: All the korbanot, whether of the tzibur (the community) or of the yachid (the individual), are of four kinds: olah (burnt offering), chatat (sin offering), asham (guilt offering), and shelamim (peace offering).
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:3: Furthermore, there are three other types of korban of an individual (korban yachid): the Pesach offering, the bechor (firstborn animal), and the maaser (animal tithe).
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:4: All the public korbanot (offerings of the tzibur) are either an olah (burnt offering) or a chatat (sin offering). There are no shelamim (peace offerings) among the public korbanot, except for the two lambs that come with the loaves of the waving (lechem hatenufah) on Shavuot. These are called "the shelamim sacrifices of the tzibur." The tzibur never brings an asham (guilt offering), and never brings a bird.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:8: Every olah (burnt offering) of an animal comes only from males. It may come from sheep, from goats, and from cattle, whether adult or young; and from turtledoves and young pigeons, in which case either a male or a female is acceptable.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 1:9: The chatat (sin offering) comes from these five species, from males and from females, from adults and from young animals.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 2:1: The wine and the fine flour that are brought with a korban are called nesachim (libations). The fine flour alone is called minchat nesachim (the meal-offering of libations). Minchat nesachim requires neither tenufah (waving), nor hagashah (bringing near to the altar), nor levonah (frankincense), but it does require salt. All of it is burned on the outer altar. The wine is poured out on the altar, but it is not placed on the fire. Rather, the kohen lifts his hand and pours it on the yesod (the base of the altar), and it flows down to the shitin (the drainage channels below the altar).
Maaseh HaKorbanot 4:1: All the korbanot may be offered only during the day, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:38), "On the day He commanded the Children of Israel to offer their korbanot" – by day, and not at night. Therefore, zevachim (slaughtered offerings) may be slaughtered only during the day, and their blood may be sprinkled only on the day of the slaughter, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:16), "On the day he offers his sacrifice" – the offering must take place on the day of the slaughter. Once the sun has set, the blood becomes disqualified.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 5:1: We have already explained that the slaughter of sacrificial animals is valid when performed by non-kohanim, and that from the receiving of the blood onward, the service is a commandment of the priesthood. For all the offerings, the blood must be received in a sacred vessel (kli shareis) by the hand of a kohen. However, the place of their slaughter and the place where their blood is received is not the same for all of them.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 5:11: All of the chatat offerings that are burned have their blood brought inside into the Heichal (the Sanctuary), and the blood is sprinkled there, as is explicitly stated in the Torah. The remainder of the blood, he pours out on the western base of the outer Mizbe'ach (altar), which is the first part of it he encounters upon exiting the Heichal.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 5:19:
All the hides of kodshei kodashim (offerings of the most sacred order) belong to the kohanim, whether from the korbanot of the tzibur (community) or the korbanot of the yachid (individual), as it is stated (Vayikra 7:8): "the hide of the olah which he offered." But the hides of kodashim kalim (offerings of lesser sanctity) belong to the owners.

Any olah whose flesh the altar did not acquire, its hide the kohanim do not acquire, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:8): "the olah of a man" — an olah that was offered up for a man.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 5:6: The olah, the asham, and the shelamim, whether of an individual or of the tzibur, are alike in the throwing of their blood upon the Mizbeach; the throwing of the blood of all three is the same as that of the olah. How does he do it? The kohen takes the blood in a basin and throws from it, from the basin, two throwings onto two corners of the Mizbeach, diagonally, from the midpoint of the Mizbeach downward: onto the northeastern corner and onto the southwestern corner. When the blood is thrown upon the corner, he intends that the blood wrap around the corners in the shape of a gam (the letter gimel and the letter mem), so that the blood of the two applications will be found on all four walls of the Mizbeach, because it is stated regarding the olah and the shelamim (Vayikra 7:2; Vayikra 9:18) "all around," and the same law applies to the asham. The remainder of the blood is poured out onto the southern base (yesod) of the Mizbeach.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 5:8: He must dip his finger [into the blood] for each and every horn [of the altar]. When he finishes applying the blood to one horn, he wipes his finger on the rim of the basin, and afterward he dips a second time. This is because the remainder of the blood on his finger is invalid for applying to another horn.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 6:1: It is a positive commandment to perform the olah (burnt offering) according to its law as written in the Torah. How is the olah performed? One slaughters it and sprinkles its blood, as we have explained. One then flays it, cuts it into its pieces, and burns all the pieces on the altar, as it is stated (Vayikra 1:9): "And the kohen shall cause all of it to go up in smoke on the altar."
Maaseh HaKorbanot 6:20:
How was the olah of a bird (olat ha'of) performed? The kohen would ascend the ramp, turn to the sovev (the ledge surrounding the altar), and come to the southeast corner. There he would perform melikah (nipping) on the bird's head, opposite its neck, and sever the head completely. If he did not sever it, the korban is invalid.

He would then squeeze out the blood of the head and the blood of the body against the wall of the altar, above the line (chut) in the middle of the altar. If he squeezed out the blood of the head but did not squeeze out the blood of the body, the korban is invalid. If he squeezed out the blood of the body but did not squeeze out the blood of the head, it is valid.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 6:22: (Vayikra 1:17) "And he shall tear it open by its wings" – with his hand, without a knife. He does not need to separate [the wings from the body], as it is stated (Vayikra 1:17) "he shall not separate it"; but if he did separate it, it is valid. He then dips it in salt and throws it onto the fires [of the altar]. If he did not remove the crop, nor the feathers, nor the innards, and did not dip it in salt – whatever he changed in it after the squeezing out of the blood, it is valid.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 7:6:
How was the chatat of a bird performed? The kohen performs melikah (pinching the neck) at the southwestern corner of the Altar, as we have explained. He cuts with his fingernail until he severs the two simanim (the windpipe and the gullet), or the majority of one of them, but he does not separate the head from the body. If he separates it, he disqualifies the korban and is liable to lashes, as it is stated (Vayikra 5:8): "And he shall pinch its head from opposite its nape, but shall not divide it."

He then sprinkles some of its blood on the wall of the Altar, below its midpoint. The remainder of the blood is squeezed out upon the base, as it is stated (Vayikra 5:9): "And the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the Altar." From this we learn that the application of the blood is on the wall, whose remainder is drained to the base, and this is the lower wall.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 9:17: How is the bread that he brings with the todah (thanksgiving offering) prepared? He takes twenty issaron of fine flour and makes of it ten issarons of leavened bread and ten of matzah. The ten issarons of leavened bread he makes into ten loaves.
Maaseh HaKorbanot 9:6: How is the procedure of these three (korbanot) performed? One slaughters the animal and sprinkles its blood as we have explained. Then one flays it and removes the emurin (the portions burned on the altar). After that, one cuts up the meat and separates the breast and the right thigh. The owners place the emurin, together with the breast and the thigh, into their own hands, and the kohen places his hand beneath the hands of the owners and waves everything before Hashem in the east. Likewise, anything that requires waving is waved in the east.
Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1: There are four who are called "those lacking atonement" (mechusrei kapparah): the zavah, the woman who has given birth, the zav, and the metzora. Why are they called "those lacking atonement"? Because each of them, even after becoming pure from his impurity, immersing, and waiting until nightfall, is still lacking: his purification is not yet complete so that he may eat sacrificial foods (kodashim) until he brings his korban. Before he brings his atonement, he is forbidden to eat kodashim, as we explained in the laws of Pesulei HaMukdashin.
Mechusrei Kapparah 1:2:
A convert who has circumcised and immersed but has not yet brought his korban: even though he is forbidden to eat kodashim (sacred offerings) until he brings his korban, he is not one of those who lack atonement (mechusrei kapparah). For his korban is what holds back his becoming a complete convert and being like all other fit members of Israel, and for this reason he does not eat kodashim, since he has not yet been made like the fit members of Israel. Once he brings his korban and becomes a fit Israelite, he eats kodashim.

If he brought one pereidah (one bird of the pair) in the morning, he may eat kodashim in the evening, and he is to bring the second pereidah. For the korban of a convert is an olah of an animal, or two young doves, or two turtledoves, and both of them are an olah, as we explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot.
Mechusrei Kapparah 2:1: The zav spoken of in the Torah is a seminal emission that comes from illnesses of the hollow organs, in which it collects. When the zov emerges, it does not come out with difficulty as semen does, and its emission brings neither desire nor pleasure. Rather, it is drawn out and flows, like barley dough, dull in color, like the white of an egg that is putrid (muzeret). But semen is white and bound together, like the white of an egg that is not putrid.
Mechusrei Kapparah 4:1:
When a metzora is healed of his tzara'at, after he has been purified with cedar wood, hyssop, scarlet wool, and the two birds, and all his flesh has been shaved and he has immersed, after all this he enters Jerusalem and counts seven days. On the seventh day he shaves a second time, like the first shaving, and immerses. He is then a tevul yom (one who has immersed and awaits nightfall), and his sun sets (he becomes fully pure at nightfall). On the next day, the eighth, he immerses a second time, and afterward his korbanot are offered.

Why does he immerse on the eighth day, when he already immersed the previous evening? Because he was accustomed to impurity during the days of his isolation, and is not careful about tumah, and perhaps he became impure after he immersed. Therefore he immerses on the eighth day in the Ezrat Nashim, in the Lishkat HaMetzora'im (Chamber of the Metzora'im), for there, even if he has not kept his mind off becoming impure, (his immersion is valid).
Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2:
If he was delayed and did not shave on the seventh day, but shaved on the eighth or after several days, then on the day that he shaves he immerses, and after nightfall he becomes tahor; the next day he brings his korbanot, after immersing a second time, as we have explained.

How is this done for him? The metzora stands outside the Israelites' Courtyard, opposite the eastern entrance, at the threshold of the Nikanor Gate, facing west. There all those who lack atonement stand when they are being purified, and there the sotot are given to drink.

The kohen takes the asham of the metzora while it is still alive and waves it together with the log of oil in the east, in the manner of all wave-offerings. If he waved this one separately and that one separately, he has fulfilled the obligation.

Afterward he brings the asham of the metzora to the entrance, and the metzora places both his hands into the Courtyard and performs semichah on it, and it is slaughtered immediately. Two kohanim receive its blood. One receives it in a vessel and throws it upon the Altar; the other receives it in his right hand, pours it into his left hand, and sprinkles it with his right finger. If he deviated and received it first in the left hand, it is disqualified.

The kohen who received part of the blood in a vessel brings it and throws it upon the Altar first. Afterward the kohen who received the blood in his palm comes to the metzora, the kohen being inside and the metzora outside. The metzora inserts his head, and the kohen places some of the blood in his palm on the lobe of the metzora's right ear. Afterward the metzora inserts his right hand, and the kohen places blood on the thumb of his hand; afterward he inserts his right foot, and the kohen places blood on the big toe of his foot. If he placed it on the left, he has not fulfilled the obligation. Afterward he offers the metzora's chatat and olah.

Mechusrei Kapparah 4:3: The remainder of the log of oil may be eaten only in the Azarah (Temple courtyard), by male kohanim, like the other kodshei kodashim (offerings of the highest sanctity), since it was compared to the asham (guilt offering). It is forbidden to eat from the log of oil until one has applied from it the sevenfold sprinkling and the application to the thumbs (the "behonot," the thumb and big toe). If one ate before this, he is punished with lashes, like one who eats sacrificial food before the blood has been sprinkled.
Shegagot 10:1:
Six people are commanded to bring a korban olah v'yored (a variable offering, which depends on the means of the one who brings it). They are:

1. The metzora (one afflicted with tzaraat).
2. A woman who has given birth.
3. One who took an oath of testimony (shevuat ha'edut), whether intentionally or inadvertently.
4. One who took an oath of utterance (shevuat bitui) falsely, inadvertently.
5. A tamei person who inadvertently ate kodesh (sacred food).

Shegagot 12:1:
Any matter for which one is liable to bring a chatat kevu'ah (a fixed sin-offering) for its inadvertent transgression: if the Great Beit Din erred in a ruling and ruled to permit it, and the people erred in reliance on their ruling and acted, relying on their ruling, and afterward it became known to the Beit Din that they had erred, the Beit Din is obligated to bring a korban chatat for their error in ruling. This is so even though they themselves did not perform any act, for the act of the Beit Din is not considered at all; whether they acted or did not act, the liability is only for their ruling. The rest of the people are exempt from the korban, even though they are the ones who acted, because they relied on the Beit Din.

What is the korban that is brought for this error? If they erred regarding idolatry and ruled accordingly, they bring a bull as an olah and a goat as a chatat from each and every tribe. This korban is the one stated in the portion of Shelach Lecha, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:24): "And it shall be, if it was done unwittingly, without the knowledge of the congregation." From the oral tradition they learned that this speaks of an error regarding idolatry.

If they erred and ruled regarding the other prohibitions punishable by karet, for whose inadvertent transgression one is liable to bring a chatat kevu'ah, each and every tribe brings a bull as a chatat. This is what is stated in the portion of Vayikra, as it is said (Vayikra 4:13): "And if the whole congregation of Israel shall err."

You thus learn that if the Great Beit Din erred in a ruling regarding idolatry, the whole community brings twelve bulls as olot and twelve goats as chatat offerings. These are burned, since their blood is brought inside, and they are called the "goats of idolatry."

If they erred regarding the other mitzvot, they bring twelve bulls as chatat offerings, and these are burned because their blood is brought inside. Each one of these bulls is called "the bull of the unwitting matter of the tzibur (community)," as it is said (Vayikra 4:14): "and the congregation
Shegagot 1:1: Anyone who unintentionally transgresses one of the negative commandments that involves a physical act, and for which one is liable to karet (excision) if done intentionally, is obligated to bring a korban chatat (sin-offering). And it is a positive commandment that he bring his chatat for his unintentional transgression.
Shegagot 2:1:
A person is not liable for a chatat (sin-offering) for an unintentional transgression unless he was unintentional from beginning to end. But if he acted unintentionally at the beginning and intentionally at the end, or intentionally at the beginning and unintentionally at the end, he is exempt from a korban chatat.

How so? For example, if one carried an object from one domain to another on Shabbat, and he lifted it intentionally but put it down unintentionally, or he lifted it unintentionally but put it down intentionally, he is exempt. He is liable only if he lifts it unintentionally and puts it down unintentionally. The same applies to all similar cases.
Shegagot 5:1:
One who has relations with a forbidden partner (ervah) many times in a single lapse of awareness (he'elem) is liable for only one chatat, even if many days passed between one act of relations and the next. Since it was not made known to him in the interim, and she is one and the same body, all of it is considered one single unintentional transgression (shegagah), and he is liable for only one chatat.

But if he transgressed unintentionally with her, and afterward it was made known to him, and he again transgressed unintentionally with that same woman and had relations with her, and afterward it was made known to him, and he again transgressed unintentionally with that same woman and had relations with her, he is liable for each and every act of relations. For the times he was made aware divide the unintentional transgressions.
Shegagot 8:1: For any sin whose unintentional transgression obligates a fixed chatat (a set sin-offering), one is obligated to bring an asham talui (a suspended guilt-offering) when he is uncertain whether he sinned. What is meant by "uncertain"? If he is unsure whether he unintentionally transgressed in a particular matter or did not, he is commanded to bring an asham, as it is stated (Vayikra 5:17): "and he did not know, yet he is guilty and shall bear his iniquity," and (Vayikra 5:18): "And he shall bring an unblemished ram from the flock, at your valuation, for an asham." This is called an asham talui because it atones for the doubt and suspends [the matter] for him until it becomes known to him with certainty that he sinned unintentionally, and then he must bring his chatat.
Temidin uMusafin 10:6:
During all seven days of the festival of Sukkot, water is poured as a libation upon the altar. This is a halachah leMoshe miSinai (a law given to Moshe at Sinai). The water was poured together with the libation of wine of the morning tamid (daily offering), with the water being poured by itself.

Wait — let me render this accurately and cleanly:

During all seven days of the festival of Sukkot, water is poured as a libation upon the altar. This is a halachah leMoshe miSinai (a law transmitted to Moshe at Sinai). Along with the libation of wine of the morning tamid (daily offering), he would pour the water by itself.
Temidin uMusafin 1:1: It is a positive commandment to offer two lambs as olot (burnt offerings) every day, and these are called the temidin (daily offerings). One is offered in the morning and one in the afternoon (bein ha'arbayim), as it is stated (Bamidbar 28:3): "two a day, a continual olah," etc.
Temidin uMusafin 2:1: It is a positive commandment that a fire burn continually on the Altar, as it is stated (Vayikra 6:6): "A perpetual fire shall be kept burning on the Altar." Even though the fire descended from heaven, it is a mitzvah to bring fire from a commoner (hedyot), as it is stated (Vayikra 1:7): "And the sons of Aharon the kohen shall place fire on the Altar."
Temidin uMusafin 3:18: It is a positive commandment to offer the chavitei kohen gadol (the griddle-cakes of the High Priest) every day, half in the morning with the morning tamid, and half in the afternoon with the afternoon tamid. Kneading them and baking them override Shabbat and tumah (ritual impurity), like every korban that has a fixed time, as it is stated (Vayikra 6:14), "tufinei" – meaning that it should be baked properly, and not be baked from the previous evening. Moreover, if it were baked from the previous evening, it would become disqualified through lina (being left overnight), since the marcheshet (the deep pan) is among the sacred vessels, as we have explained.
Temidin uMusafin 4:1: All of these services that are performed each day were assigned by lottery (payis). How was this done? All the kohanim of the paternal house (beit av) serving that day would enter the Lishkat HaGazit (the Chamber of Hewn Stone) after dawn had risen, dressed in the priestly garments. The official in charge of the lotteries would be with them, and they would stand in a circle. The official would remove the turban from the head of one of them and put it back; this was the man from whom they began the count. They then cast lots, as will be explained.
Temidin uMusafin 4:2: And the men who serve in it go out to the service. The rest of the kohanim hand over the garments to the attendants, who strip them of the sacred garments. They would leave on them only the breeches, until they put on their weekday clothes. Then they remove the sacred breeches as well, and the attendants return the garments to the niches.
Temidin uMusafin 4:3:
How is the lottery conducted? The kohanim stand in a circle and agree upon a number, eighty, a hundred, a thousand, or any number they agree upon. The appointed official says to them, "Put out your fingers," and they extend their fingers, one or two. If one extends three, they count three for him. They do not extend a thumb in the Temple because of deceivers, since the thumb is short and it is easy to extend it or to fold it in. One who extends a thumb is not counted for it.

The appointed official begins counting from the known man who removed his headdress first. He counts on their fingers and goes around again and again until he completes the number they agreed upon. The man at whose finger the number is completed is the one who is chosen in the first lottery for the avodah (Temple service).
Temidin uMusafin 5:1: It is a positive commandment to arrange the lechem hapanim (the showbread) on the table before Hashem in the Heichal every Shabbat, as it is stated (Vayikra 24:8): "Every Shabbat day he shall arrange it," etc.
Temidin uMusafin 5:2: It is a clear matter in the Torah that there are twelve loaves, each loaf made from two esronim (a tenth of an ephah of flour). They arrange it in two rows, six loaves in each row, one loaf on top of another. Between each two loaves are three golden tubes, so that the air can circulate through it. He supports each row with two rods. Beside each row they place a vessel containing a handful of frankincense, as it is stated (Vayikra 24:7): "And you shall place pure frankincense upon each row." This vessel is called a bazach. Thus there are two handfuls of frankincense in the two bazichin. The bazichin had bases so that they could be set down on the table.
Temidin uMusafin 7:3: On Pesach, a musaf offering (an additional offering) is brought every day. From the first day until the seventh day, it is like the musaf of Rosh Chodesh: two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs, all of them olot, and a se'ir chatat (a goat sin-offering) that is eaten. On the second day of Pesach, which is the sixteenth of Nissan, in addition to the musaf of every day, a lamb is brought as an olah, together with the omer of the waving. This is a mincha of the tzibur (the community), as we have explained.
Temidin uMusafin 8:1:
On the fiftieth day of the counting of the Omer is the festival of Shavuot, which is also called Atzeret. On this day they offer a musaf (additional offering) like the musaf of Rosh Chodesh: two young bulls, one ram, and seven lambs, all of them olot (burnt offerings), and a se'ir chatat (goat as a sin offering). These are the offerings stated in the Book of Bamidbar (Chumash HaPekudim), and they are the musaf of the day.

In addition to the musaf, on this day they also bring a new mincha (meal offering), the shtei halechem (two loaves). Together with the loaves they offer one young bull, two rams, and seven lambs, all of them olot, and a se'ir chatat, and two lambs as a zevach shelamim (peace offering). These are the offerings stated in the Book of Vayikra.

It therefore turns out that what is offered on this day, beyond the two tamidim (daily offerings), is three young bulls, three rams, and fourteen lambs, twenty animals in all as olot; two se'irei chatat (sin-offering goats), which are eaten; and two lambs as shelamim, which are eaten.

Vayikra 5:9: He shall sprinkle some of the blood of the chatat (sin-offering) upon the wall of the altar, and the remainder of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a chatat.
Vayikra 6:13-15:
This is the korban of Aharon and his sons which they shall offer to Hashem on the day he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual mincha (meal offering), half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening.

It shall be made on a griddle with oil; it shall be brought well soaked. You shall bring it as baked pieces of a mincha, broken into bits, and offer it as a pleasing aroma to Hashem.

And the anointed kohen from among his sons who succeeds him shall make it, as an eternal statute to Hashem; it shall be burnt entirely.
Vayikra 6:16: Every mincha (meal offering) of a kohen shall be burnt entirely; it shall not be eaten.
Vayikra 6:18: Speak to Aharon and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the chatat (sin-offering): in the place where the olah (burnt-offering) is slaughtered, the chatat shall be slaughtered before Hashem; it is kodshei kodashim (most holy).
Vayikra 6:19: The kohen who performs the sin-offering with it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.
Vayikra 6:23: But any chatat (sin-offering) whose blood is brought into the Ohel Mo'ed (Tent of Meeting) to make atonement in the Kodesh (the Sanctuary) shall not be eaten; it shall be burned in fire.
Vayikra 7:12-13: If he offers it for a thanksgiving (todah), then together with the thanksgiving offering he shall offer unleavened loaves (challot) mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers (rekikim) spread with oil, and loaves of fine flour well soaked, mixed with oil. Along with loaves of leavened bread he shall present his offering, together with his thanksgiving feast offering of shelamim.
Vayikra 7:12-16: If he offers it for a thanksgiving (todah), then along with the sacrifice of thanksgiving he shall offer unleavened cakes mixed with oil, unleavened wafers spread with oil, and cakes of fine flour soaked and mixed with oil. With cakes of leavened bread he shall present his offering, together with his thanksgiving sacrifice of shelamim. From it he shall present one of each offering as a gift (terumah) to Hashem; it shall belong to the kohen who sprinkles the blood of the shelamim. The flesh of his thanksgiving sacrifice of shelamim shall be eaten on the day of his offering; he shall not leave any of it until morning. But if the sacrifice of his offering is a neder (vow) or a nedavah (freewill offering), it shall be eaten on the day he presents his sacrifice, and on the next day what remains of it may be eaten.
Vayikra 7:15: And the flesh of the zevach of his todah shelamim shall be eaten on the day of his korban; he shall not leave any of it until morning.
Vayikra 7:15-16: And the flesh of the zevach (sacrifice) of his shelamim (peace offering) of thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering; he shall not leave any of it until morning. But if the zevach of his offering is a neder (vow) or a nedavah (voluntary offering), it shall be eaten on the day that he brings near his zevach, and on the next day, and what remains of it may be eaten.
Vayikra 7:16: But if the sacrifice of his korban is a vow-offering (neder) or a freewill offering (nedavah), it shall be eaten on the day he brings near his sacrifice, and on the next day, and what remains of it may be eaten.
Vayikra 7:18: And if any of the flesh of his shelamim offering is eaten at all on the third day, it shall not be accepted; it shall not be credited to the one who offers it. It shall be piggul (an abominable thing), and the person who eats of it shall bear his iniquity.
Vayikra 7:30: His own hands shall bring the fire-offerings of Hashem; he shall bring the fat together with the chest, so that the chest may be waved as a wave-offering before Hashem.
Vayikra 7:31-34: The kohen shall burn the fat on the altar, and the breast shall belong to Aharon and his sons. And the right thigh you shall give as a terumah (a raised gift) to the kohen, from your shelamim sacrifices. The one among the sons of Aharon who offers the blood of the shelamim and the fat shall have the right thigh as his portion. For I have taken the breast of the waving (tenufah) and the thigh of the raised gift (terumah) from the children of Israel, from their shelamim sacrifices, and I have given them to Aharon the kohen and to his sons as a perpetual statute from the children of Israel.
Vayikra 7:8: And the kohen who offers a man's olah (burnt offering) — the hide of the olah which he has offered shall belong to that kohen; it shall be his.
